public_rationale: Original surveys support substantial public demand for AI safeguards. Gallup found 80% favored retaining safety rules, while Ipsos found 68% support for regulation for public safety and 61% for economic stability. These results depend on wording and do not establish what every poll Marcus saw reported. The personal qualifier prevents a conclusive whole-claim verdict. His doubt about chip sales is not a firm forecast.
limitations: The two-thirds benchmark is an evaluator interpretation.
Government regulation, shared industry standards, and specific safeguards are not interchangeable.
The evidence supports the broad public-opinion concern more clearly than the universal personal statement.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Every poll Marcus has seen shows the vast majority of the public wanting AI regulation, and he doubts people will be fond of selling advanced chips to China.

statement.excerpt: Every poll I have seen shows the vast majority of the public wanting AI regulation, and I doubt people will be fond of selling fancy chips to China.
statement.document_title: Is the White House’s AI Policy Coherent?

from_speaker: I doubt people will be fond of selling fancy chips to China
our_interpretation: The checkable public component concerns American support for AI regulation in polling available before publication.
Use 2025 polling as the recent public-evidence window for the ongoing observation; this does not identify or exhaust the polls Marcus personally saw.
Two-thirds support is an evaluator benchmark for a large majority, not a threshold supplied by Marcus.
Support for some AI rules, support for government regulation, and support for a particular regulatory proposal are different measures.
The chip-sales clause expresses a doubt without a deadline or firm outcome commitment and is not separately scored as a forecast.
criteria.support_condition: The polls Marcus refers to can be identified, and their representative US results consistently show clear large majorities favoring AI regulation under comparable questions.
criteria.contradiction_condition: An identified poll within Marcus's stated set fails to show a clear large majority on a comparable regulation question. A poll outside that set cannot alone disprove his report of what he saw.

evidence.explanation: The survey, fielded April 25–May 5, found 80% preferred maintaining government safety and data-security rules even at the cost of slower development. However, a separate question found 54% selected government as a rule-setting body, demonstrating that the formulation matters.

evidence.locator: About the Study, first paragraph; findings in second opening paragraph
evidence.explanation: The August 13–18 poll found 68% favored government regulation for public safety and 61% for economic stability. This qualifies any claim of uniformly overwhelming support across question wording, but does not establish that Marcus saw this poll.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Identification of the polls Marcus meant, with their original questions and results, would allow assessment of the regulation clause. The chip-sales clause would require a definite, separately stated prediction.
